raw_case_text:
A 27-year-old woman (gravida 2, para 1) underwent a routine ultrasound examination at 19 weeks' gestation and fetal ascites was observed. She was referred to a tertiary center and her serology was positive for CMV-IgM. She was then transferred to our center for further treatment. She was confirmed as having primary CMV infection during pregnancy by positive CMV-DNA (3.4 x 105 copies/ml) of fetal ascites and low CMV-IgG avidity (16.6%) at 20 weeks' gestation. Fetal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) at 27 weeks showed massive ascites and compressed low-intensity lungs (Figure 1A). We performed fetal therapies, including intravenous immunoglobulin to the mother [22, 24, and 25 gestational weeks (GW)], ascites removal followed by fetal intraperitoneal injection of immunoglobulin (20, 21, 23, 26, 27, and 29 GW) and albumin (22, 26, 28, 30, and 31 GW); and amniotic fluid removal for polyhydramnios, which occurred since 28 weeks (28, 30, and 31 GW). At 31 GW and 0 days, she gave birth to a female neonate (birth weight of 1,824 g; Apgar scores of 4 and 6 at 1 and 5 min, respectively) via emergent cesarean section because of signs of threatened premature delivery after cordocentesis. The neonate was tracheally intubated soon after birth, and her heart rate gradually increased. Her abdomen was massively distended with palpable fluctuation, but no petechiae were detected. A blood test showed mild leukopenia (3,800/mul), anemia (86 g/l), thrombocytopenia (6.1 x 104/mul), hypogammaglobulinemia (3.46 g/l), and hypoalbuminemia (24 g/l). Despite the normal aspartate aminotransferase (66 IU/l) and alanine aminotransferase (5 IU/l) levels, the level of total protein (29 g/l), fibrinogen (680 mg/l), and prothrombin time (<10%) were significantly decreased, suggesting liver failure from congenital CMV infections. An X-ray showed marked reduction in lung volume (Figure 1B), with an increase in abdominal volume by massive ascites. Abdominal echo revealed hepatomegaly and brain echo revealed periventricular hyperechogenicity but could not detect ventriculomegaly and calcifications.
We removed 300 ml of peritoneal fluid by peritoneocentesis to lower the lung compression. However, her respiratory status gradually deteriorated, despite the highest ventilator settings, with signs of persistent pulmonary hypertension. Therefore, we started inhaled nitric oxide 6 h after birth, but she developed pneumopericardium at 8 h. At 14 h after birth, she eventually died because of pulmonary hypoplasia. Autopsy imaging showed ventriculomegaly and intracranial calcification, in addition to a reduced lung volume (Figure 1C). Positive CMV-DNA (blood: 66 copies/106 white blood cells, urine: 1.2 x 107 copies/ml) confirmed congenital CMV infection.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 27-year-old pregnant woman (gravida 2, para 1) was referred at 19-20 weeks' gestation for massive fetal ascites and polyhydramnios, subsequently delivering a preterm female neonate at 31 weeks' gestation with severe abdominal distension and respiratory failure.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Routine prenatal ultrasound at 19 weeks' gestation detected fetal ascites, and maternal/fetal workup at 20 weeks confirmed primary gestational CMV infection (positive maternal CMV-IgM, low maternal CMV-IgG avidity 16.6%, and fetal ascites CMV-DNA 3.4 x 10^5 copies/mL) with polyhydramnios developing at 28 weeks. Despite serial intrauterine fetal therapies—maternal IVIG (22, 24, 25 GW), fetal paracentesis with fetal intraperitoneal immunoglobulin (20, 21, 23, 26, 27, 29 GW) and albumin injections (22, 26, 28, 30, 31 GW), and amnioreduction (28, 30, 31 GW)—threatened preterm labor after cordocentesis at 31 weeks 0 days required emergency cesarean delivery of a 1,824 g female infant with massive ascites and severe respiratory failure.
subjective.past_medical_history: Mother: 27-year-old gravida 2, para 1 with primary CMV infection diagnosed at 19-20 weeks' gestation. Neonate: preterm female born at 31 weeks 0 days' gestation (birth weight 1,824 g) with in utero congenital CMV infection.
subjective.review_of_systems: Maternal/fetal: fetal ascites (from 19 GW) and polyhydramnios (from 28 GW). Neonatal: severe neonatal respiratory distress and massive abdominal distension.

objective.physical_examination: Female neonate at birth (31w0d): birth weight 1,824 g, Apgar scores 4 at 1 min and 6 at 5 min, immediately intubated; massively distended abdomen with palpable fluid wave (fluctuation), no cutaneous petechiae.
objective.routine_investigations: Maternal serology at 20 GW: positive CMV-IgM and low CMV-IgG avidity (16.6%). Neonatal labs at birth: WBC 3,800/uL, hemoglobin 86 g/L, platelets 6.1 x 10^4/uL, IgG 3.46 g/L (hypogammaglobulinemia), albumin 24 g/L, total protein 29 g/L, AST 66 IU/L, ALT 5 IU/L, fibrinogen 680 mg/L, and prothrombin time <10%. Neonatal chest/abdominal radiograph showed markedly reduced lung volumes and massive abdominal distension from ascites; abdominal ultrasound showed hepatomegaly; cranial ultrasound showed periventricular hyperechogenicity.
objective.advanced_workup: Fetal paracentesis at 20 GW showed fetal ascites CMV-DNA of 3.4 x 10^5 copies/mL; fetal MRI at 27 GW showed massive fetal ascites and compressed low-signal hypoplastic lungs. Neonatal quantitative CMV-DNA PCR was positive in blood (66 copies/10^6 WBCs) and urine (1.2 x 10^7 copies/mL). Postmortem autopsy CT/imaging confirmed severe pulmonary hypoplasia, ventriculomegaly, and intracranial calcifications.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis of severe symptomatic congenital cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection with fetal ascites, hepatic synthetic failure, intracranial calcifications/ventriculomegaly, and fatal pulmonary hypoplasia, confirmed prenatally by maternal low-avidity CMV-IgG (16.6%) and fetal ascites CMV-DNA (3.4 x 10^5 copies/mL) and postnatally by neonatal blood (66 copies/10^6 WBCs) and urine (1.2 x 10^7 copies/mL) CMV-DNA PCR and postmortem imaging. Despite prenatal maternal IVIG, serial fetal paracenteses with intraperitoneal IVIG/albumin infusions, neonatal mechanical ventilation, 300 mL therapeutic paracentesis, and inhaled nitric oxide for persistent pulmonary hypertension, the neonate developed pneumopericardium at 8 hours of life and died at 14 hours of life from severe pulmonary hypoplasia.
